# assemblies.py
*`src/pySEA/rayTEM/assemblies.py`*

## Overview

`assemblies.py` defines `MicroscopeSection` (an ordered sequence of `Element` objects) and `Microscope` (an ordered sequence of `MicroscopeSection` objects). Both support propagation, visualization, serialization, and name-based indexing. The hierarchy is strictly bottom-up: propagation delegates from `Microscope` → `MicroscopeSection` → each `Element`.

See [elements.md](elements.md) for the Element base class and ray column conventions.

---

## Module-level functions

### `load_section(filename)`

Loads a `MicroscopeSection` from a `.pkl` file (via `pickle.load`). If the filename contains `".sea"`, loads via `MicroscopeSection.from_sea()` instead.

### `load_microscope(filename)`

Loads a `Microscope` from either a `.sea` file (via `SEASerializable.from_sea`) or a `.json` file (plain JSON produced by `Microscope.save`). After loading from either format, reconstructs properly typed Python objects: the JSON/sea data stores element `kind` strings which are mapped back to concrete classes (`Drift`, `Lens`, `Source`, etc.) via a lookup table. Filters kwargs to match each class's `__init__` signature to handle version mismatches gracefully.

---

## MicroscopeSection

A named, ordered list of `Element` objects representing one functional segment of the column (e.g. the condenser system, the projector lenses). On construction, the section auto-inserts `Drift` elements to fill any positional gaps between elements, so you can specify element positions absolutely rather than sequentially.

### `MicroscopeSection.__init__(self, name, elements, position, ignoreLensThickness)`

Iterates through the provided `elements` list and fills gaps:
- If an element has `position=None`, it is placed at the current running length.
- If the running length is less than the next element's position, a `Drift` is inserted to bridge the gap.
- `ignoreLensThickness=True` treats all lenses as thin (zero thickness), useful for quick checks.

After construction, `self.elements` is the gap-filled list and `self.length` is the total section length.

### `MicroscopeSection.index(self, item)`

Returns the integer index of the element named `item` within `self.elements`.

### `MicroscopeSection.__getitem__ / __setitem__ / __delitem__`

Name-based access: `section["PL1"]` returns the element named `"PL1"`. Slice access `section["sample":]` returns a new `MicroscopeSection` containing elements from `"sample"` onward, with positions re-zeroed. This is used to extract sub-sections for downstream analysis (e.g. fit only the projectors given a calibrated pre-specimen section).

### `MicroscopeSection.insert(self, index, element)`

Two modes:
- `index` is an integer: standard list insertion.
- `index` is a float coordinate: finds the `Drift` element spanning that coordinate, splits it, and inserts the new element at the specified z position. The surrounding drifts are shortened to maintain total section length.

### `MicroscopeSection.append(self, element)`

Appends an element at the end of the section.

### `MicroscopeSection.wobble(self, r0, elementIndex, func, kwargName, valRange, numSteps)`

Sweeps one element parameter over `valRange` in `numSteps` steps. At each step replaces `elements[elementIndex]` with `func(**{kwargName: v})` and calls `propagate_ray`. Returns a list of ray arrays (one per step) at the exit of the section. Used to generate the data for manual or automated fitting.

### `MicroscopeSection.named_positions`

Property. Returns `{element.name: element.position}` for all non-None-named elements. Used by `plot2D` to draw vertical annotation lines at named planes (sample, CCD, etc.).

### `MicroscopeSection.propagate_ray(self, r0, z, verbose)`

Iterates through `self.elements` in order, passing the output of each element as input to the next. Elements with zero length (thin lenses, Source) don't add a new entry to the ray history — their output overwrites the previous entry, keeping the ray array compact. Per element the driver calls `apply_intensity` (before the ray transform) and `apply_rotation` (after), maintaining the parallel `.I` and `.R` arrays. After propagation, `self.rays` is `(n_planes, n_rays, 6)` (the geometric convention columns) with `self.I`/`self.R` `(n_planes, n_rays)`. Returns `self.rays`.

If `r0=None` and the first element is a `Source`, calls `Source.rays()` to generate starting rays.

### `MicroscopeSection.propagate_wave(self, wave0=None, mode='fixed', s_min=1e-3)`

The one wave driver (same element loop and plane logging as the ray path,
planes after each finite-length element or aperture). `mode='fixed'`: stacks
per-plane fields into a calibrated `(n_planes, ny, nx)` Signal on `self.wave`
(per-plane Signals on `self._wave_planes` for `Microscope` chaining).
`'scaled'`/`'hybrid'`: threads the reduced field U + frame state (s, R, τ)
and stacks onto `self.wave_scaled` as a `SignalSet` — U `(n_planes, nη, nξ)`
main Signal plus companion 1-D `s(z)`/`R(z)`/`tau(z)` (and, on hybrid runs,
`frame`) Signals on the shared unstructured plane-z axis (built by
`_stack_scaled_wavefields` → `seashells.make_scaled_wave_signalset`); on an
**anisotropic** run (a quadrupole absorbed per-axis powers) the companions
become `s_x`/`s_y`, `R_x`/`R_y`, `tau_x`/`tau_y`. On `'hybrid'` the interior
flatten/crossover/rediverge planes logged by the engine are inserted in z
order (per-axis line foci carry axis-suffixed tags). Seeds from
`Source.wave(mode=...)` when `wave0=None`. `'scaled'` raises before a
crossover (Eq 52); `'hybrid'` switches frames through it. `absorb` (default
0.1) and `crossover` (`'flat'`/`'jump'`) are threaded down to every element.

### `MicroscopeSection.propagate(self, *args, kind='ray', **kwargs)`

Unified dispatcher; `kind` ∈ ray/rays, moments/envelope/covariance, wave,
wave-scaled, wave-hybrid (underscore aliases accepted).

### `MicroscopeSection.show(self, filename, title, ylims, zlims, regenerate)`

Runs `propagate_ray` (unless `regenerate=False` and `self.rays` is already populated), then calls `plot2D` with named positions as annotations. Saves to file if `filename` is provided, otherwise displays interactively.

### `MicroscopeSection.save(self, filename)`

Saves to a `.pkl` file via `pickle`. For reproducible, human-readable storage use `Microscope.save` (JSON) or `to_sea` (sea_eco).

## Microscope

A full microscope model composed of ordered `MicroscopeSection` objects. On construction, auto-inserts drift tails into sections to fill gaps between consecutive sections (analogous to what `MicroscopeSection.__init__` does for elements).

### `Microscope.__init__(self, name, sections)`

Checks each pair of consecutive sections: if the end of section N is before the start of section N+1, a `Drift` is appended to section N. If a section has `position=0` (unset), it is positioned to start at the end of the previous section.

### `Microscope.index(self, item)`

Searches for `item` by name: first among section names (returns integer index), then among element names within sections (returns `(section_index, element_index)` tuple). Used by `__getitem__` for string-based access.

### `Microscope.__getitem__`

- Integer index: returns the nth section.
- String: finds the named section or element. Section name returns the section; element name returns a `(section_i, element_j)` tuple which can then index back into `self.sections[i].elements[j]`.
- Slice: if section-level (`"OLs":`) returns a new `Microscope` with those sections. If element-level (`"sample":`), trims the first section to start at that element and re-zeros positions.

### `Microscope.insert(self, index, elementOrSection)`

Coordinate-based insertion. Finds which section spans `index` and delegates to `MicroscopeSection.insert`. If inserting a full `MicroscopeSection`, splits the host section at that coordinate into three parts.

### `Microscope.adjust_element_length(self, element, newlength)`

Changes the length of a named element and compensates by adjusting the following element's position and length. Only works if the element is not last in its section.

### `Microscope.named_positions`

Property. Aggregates `named_positions` from all sections, offsetting each element position by its section's position. Returns one flat `{name: absolute_z}` dict for the whole column.

### `Microscope.propagate_ray(self, r0, z, verbose)`

Iterates through sections in order. The exit rays of each section become the entry rays for the next. The flattened ray history across all sections is stored as `self.rays` and returned.

### `Microscope.propagate_wave(self, wave0=None, mode='fixed', s_min=1e-3)`

The one wave driver with eager re-chain: each section's exit state seeds the
next; all per-plane states flatten into `self.wave` (fixed) /
`self.wave_scaled` (scaled/hybrid SignalSet of U + s/R/tau/frame companions).
Per-plane lists on `self._wave_planes` / `self._wave_scaled_planes`. Hybrid
runs also collect `self.crossovers` — the focal-plane z positions found by
the hybrid engine (per-axis line foci included: any tag starting with
`crossover`) —
the frame-switching engine (the back-focal / image planes).

### `Microscope.wavefield_at(self, z, target_dx=None, target_shape=None)`

### `Element.transfer_block(dz=None, axis='x')` — the shared seam
The rotating-frame 2×2 `[[A, B], [C, D]]` for one transverse axis, at a
**partial** length. This is what makes planes *inside* a body exact instead of
interpolated between its faces. Each element carries its body's own law —
`Lens` and `Quadrapole` override with their harmonic forms — and the base
class handles only the two cases where no law is needed: **no focusing power**
(exact free space at any depth) and **zero length** (a thin element *is* an
impulsive kick). A finite body *with* power and no override **raises**: splitting
it into a kick between drifts is precisely the approximation the scaled wave
path was corrected to drop, so it is not done here either. Verified against
`transfer_matrix` on all 58 `basic_column` elements to 1.7e-18, with bodies'
halves composing exactly.

The walk additionally checks that a body's block is **symplectic**
(`det = 1`, i.e. Liouville). This currently catches a real problem: the thick
`Quadrapole.transfer_matrix` y-block uses `cos/sin` where a defocusing axis
needs `cosh/sinh`, giving `det = cos(2|KL|)` — 0.75 over a 30 mm body. The walk
refuses that axis rather than reporting planes that cannot be trusted; fixing
`transfer_matrix` itself is a separate change (thin and thick quadrupoles also
disagree on which axis focuses, since the thin form swaps x/y for `K > 0` and
the thick form never swaps).

### `Microscope.conjugate_planes(axis='x', method='frame', reference=None, x0=1e-6, theta0=1e-6)`
Returns `{'diff', 'image', 'z_reference', 'diff_offset', 'image_offset'}` in
**metres** — the column's two independent conjugate families: **diffraction**
(back-focal / reciprocal) planes where rays that left the reference parallel
converge (`A = 0`), and **image** planes where rays from one on-axis point of
the reference re-converge (`B = 0`). They interleave, and neither follows from
a single lens's `f`: every crossing reflects the whole system since the
reference.

`method='ray'` (default) traces the four reference rays through
`postprocessing.findPlanes` — the repo's established convention.
`method='frame'` accumulates the transfer blocks
(`_accumulate_blocks`) and solves both conditions in closed form — exact, and
**this is the same calculation the scaled wave frame performs while
propagating**, since the frame is a reference ray `(h, u) = (s, s/R)`: `s → 0`
on a flat seed is `A = 0`, on a point seed is `B = 0`. So the wave's own
`crossovers` appear here, *and* the other family is available without a second
wave run (`wavefield_at` reconstructs the field at any of them).
`method='ray'` keeps the four-reference-ray `findPlanes` trace as an
independent cross-check; the two agree exactly wherever the planes fall in
free space, and the frame walk is the correct one inside a thick body (on
`basic_column` the image plane inside OL1 differs by 188 µm).

`reference=` requires `method='frame'` (the ray trace only launches from the
column entrance) and sets the **object** plane whose conjugates are wanted — a name
from `named_positions`, a z in metres, or `None` for the column entrance.
Different references give genuinely different sets, and the two families
behave differently: moving the reference across a pure drift leaves the
diffraction family unchanged (parallel stays parallel) but moves the image
family.

### `Microscope.beam_waists(axis='x', sigma0=None)`
The **covariance** mode's planes. Transporting `Σ' = MΣMᵀ`, the RMS width is
stationary where `Σ₁₂ = 0` — a waist, with *finite* width, sitting off the
geometric focus by the emittance-driven focal shift. Returns
`{'z', 'width', 'emittance'}`; matches the analytic
`f/(1 + (f·σ_θ/σ_x)²)` to 1e-12. Note `Σ₁₂` is **quadratic** in the element
matrix, unlike the linear plane condition, so thick bodies use their own
closed form `tan(2K·dz) = −2K·Σ₁₂/(Σ₂₂ − K²Σ₁₁)` (`_waist_roots`) — which is
why `basic_column` shows waists inside the C1, OL1 and PL3 bodies.

**When planes become surfaces:** with aberrations or multipoles the conjugate
condition acquires a dependence on field radius and azimuth, so the root
becomes a surface `z(r, φ)`. See
`notes/eric/PLAN_2026-08-22_aberrated-focal-surfaces.md` — the paraxial planes
stay the reference surface, and on the wave side the frame deliberately stays
paraxial because the residual non-quadratic phase on U at the logged
diffraction plane already *is* the aberration function `χ(q)`.

**Which family does the wave see?** The scaled frame follows exactly one —
whichever its *seed* belongs to. `Source.wave` seeds `s=1, R=inf` (a parallel
wavefront = the diffraction reference ray), so `crossovers` from a hybrid run
are the **diffraction/back-focal** family. The image planes are equally
reconstructable, they just are not the frame's own singularities: get their
positions here and log them exactly by composing with the sampling knob,
`zpts=scope.conjugate_planes()['image']`. Verified on a thin two-lens
compound column: wave crossovers == ray diff family == the analytic compound
values [55.0000, 176.0000] mm to 0 nm (and **not** `z_L2 + f2` = 140 mm),
with the image plane at 150.8621 mm.

### `Microscope.subdivided(zpts)`
Returns a **new** column whose unnamed drifts are cut — `float` = maximum
drift length (metres), `Sequence` = absolute z positions to cut at — for
denser plane logging. Element order, lengths, section positions and every
named position are preserved exactly (cut drifts sum to the original length;
the copy's elements restack sequentially in `MicroscopeSection.__init__`), and
this object plus any result stored on it are untouched. Named drifts are left
whole (a name marks a plane the user asked for). Use it whenever a result's z
sampling — which is always "one plane per element exit, plus a hybrid run's
frame events" — is coarser than wanted.

`Microscope.show` covers the scaled result too: `kind='wave-scaled'` /
`'wave-hybrid'` with no `plane` draws the |ψ(x, y=0, z)| **cross-section**
(the wave analog of the ray diagram — per-plane native grids resampled onto
one x axis, element and crossover overlays; `_scaled_wave_cross_section`);
with `plane=` (logged-plane index, z in metres, or a named position like
`"sample"`) it images the reconstructed physical |ψ|² by delegating to the
wavefield Signal's own `.show()` — the same composition (not inheritance)
pattern as `kind='wave'`/`'moments'`. `zpts=` propagates a temporary
`subdivided` copy and plots from it (a float `plane` joins the cut set so that
plane is logged exactly rather than snapping to the nearest existing one),
leaving this object's own result alone.

**Where `crossovers` come from** (they are not searched for numerically): in a
converging frame the reference curvature evolves as `R(z) = R₀ + Δz`, so the
frame's collapse — the geometric focus — sits at the closed-form
`z_cross = z + |R|`. `propagate_free_scaled_hybrid` records that z when it
flattens, splits its own propagation exactly there, and logs the plane tagged
`crossover` (per-axis `crossover-x`/`crossover-y` on an anisotropic frame);
`Microscope.propagate_wave` collects those z values into `self.crossovers`
(the family the wave's frame follows — see `conjugate_planes` above for the
other one). So those focal planes are always logged exactly, independent of
drift subdivision:
`show(kind='wave-hybrid', plane=scope.crossovers[i])` lands on the i-th focal
(back-focal / diffraction) plane, and `wavefield_at` reconstructs it.

The scaled-run boundary: reconstructs the physical wave ψ(x, y) at the logged
plane nearest `z` (float or named position) via
`waveoptics.reconstruct_physical_wave` — native `|s|·Δξ` grid (Eq 41) or a
prescribed target grid via band-limited resampling (Eq 44) — returning a
standard calibrated wavefield Signal for external consumers (e.g. a multislice
package). Runs `propagate_wave(mode='hybrid')` first if no scaled result is stored.
The e^{ikz} carrier is not applied.

### `Microscope.propagate(self, *args, kind='ray', **kwargs)`

Unified dispatcher; `kind` ∈ ray/rays, moments/envelope/covariance, wave,
wave-scaled, wave-hybrid (underscore aliases accepted).

### `Microscope.show(self, filename, title, ylims, zlims, regenerate, plt_ax)`

Like `MicroscopeSection.show` but also passes a `sections` dict to `plot2D` so each section is shaded with a different background color.

### `Microscope.save(self, filename)`

Writes a human-readable JSON file with nested structure: `Microscope name → Sections → Elements`. Uses `"Microscope name"`, `"Section name"`, `"Element name"` keys (instead of bare `"name"`) to make the hierarchy self-describing. `load_microscope` knows to un-map these keys on reload.
